title: Paquita no está loca  (Paquita Is Not Crazy)

segments.t: Standing up in front of the whole auditorium, loyal assistant Magüi defends Paquita against Fernando's coldness and explains why Macarena is still on their website. When they are ordered out of the hall, Paquita refuses to leave on anyone else's terms. Listen to the Spanish first.
Perdonad un momento. Quiero decir que Paquita no está loca.
Lo que tú acabas de hacer no se hace.
Yo no sé quién eres, pero sabes muy poquito de este oficio.
A lo mejor no sé mucho de esta profesión, pero sé cómo funcionan las personas.
No tengo la culpa de que me vayan bien las cosas.
Macarena vino a verme porque tú te estás quedando antigua.
A ver si la quitas de la web.
La página web la llevo yo.
No me ha dado tiempo todavía a quitarla.
¡No la toques!
Claro que vamos a abandonar la sala, pero no porque lo digas tú.
Let's hear how Magüi stands up for Paquita.
Perdonad un momento. Quiero decir que Paquita no está loca.

'Excuse me a moment. I want to say that Paquita isn't crazy.' Magüi echoes Fernando's plural "forgive" to address the room, then answers his "madness" jab directly. Using the state word "está" before "crazy" treats it as how Paquita is acting right now.
Lo que tú acabas de hacer no se hace.

'What you've just done isn't done.' Combining "finish" with "of" and an action expresses "have just done" in everyday Spanish. At the end, literally "does not make itself" is how Spaniards say something is bad form.
Yo no sé quién eres, pero sabes muy poquito de este oficio.

'I don't know who you are, but you know very little about this profession.' Notice the irregular first-person "sé" for "I know", written with an accent to distinguish it from "se". Shrinking "little" with a diminutive ending makes Fernando's put-down sound patronisingly small.
A lo mejor no sé mucho de esta profesión, pero sé cómo funcionan las personas.

'Maybe I don't know much about this profession, but I know how people work.' Spain's favourite conversational chunk for "maybe" literally says "at the best". Both "who" in the last line and "how" here carry written accents whenever they ask an indirect question.
No tengo la culpa de que me vayan bien las cosas.

'It isn't my fault that things are going well for me.' Where English says "it isn't my fault", Spanish says "I don't have the blame". Notice how "things go well to me" puts "things" at the very end as the subject.
Macarena vino a verme porque tú te estás quedando antigua.

'Macarena came to see me because you're getting outdated.' Here "me" attaches smoothly to "to see" as one word. Pairing "staying" with "ancient" or "old-fashioned" builds the stinging phrase "falling behind the times".
A ver si la quitas de la web.

'See if you can take her off the website.' Starting with "let's see if" plus the plain present is a classic Spanish way to prod someone into doing something. "La" stands for Macarena, and "the web" is universal shorthand for an agency website.
La página web la llevo yo.

'I run the website myself.' Earlier "llevar" meant representing an actress; here the exact same word means running or managing a webpage. Putting "the webpage" first and "I" dead last shoulders all the blame away from Paquita.
No me ha dado tiempo todavía a quitarla.

'I haven't had time to take her off yet.' Instead of "I haven't had time", Spanish idiomatically says "it hasn't given me time yet". At the end, "her" hooks straight onto "to remove" as a single word.
¡No la toques!

'Don't touch her!' In a negative command to "tú", the "-ar" ending flips to "-es", and spelling changes "c" to "qu" so the hard "k" sound stays intact. Unlike affirmative commands, "her" sits in front rather than attached to the end.
Claro que vamos a abandonar la sala, pero no porque lo digas tú.

'Of course we're going to leave the hall, just not because you say so.' Opening with "clear that" gives an emphatic "of course". After "not because", Spanish switches "you say" to "digas" because Paquita is rejecting his order as the reason they are leaving. Now let's listen to the whole scene again.
Perdonad un momento. Quiero decir que Paquita no está loca.
Lo que tú acabas de hacer no se hace.
Yo no sé quién eres, pero sabes muy poquito de este oficio.
A lo mejor no sé mucho de esta profesión, pero sé cómo funcionan las personas.
No tengo la culpa de que me vayan bien las cosas.
Macarena vino a verme porque tú te estás quedando antigua.
A ver si la quitas de la web.
La página web la llevo yo.
No me ha dado tiempo todavía a quitarla.
¡No la toques!
Claro que vamos a abandonar la sala, pero no porque lo digas tú.
You heard how Spanish expresses "have just done", says "maybe" with a three-word chunk, and softens commands or protests when tensions flare. See you next time.
¡Adiós!
